title: The AI Code Problem Nobody's Talking About
summary: Security vendor monologue: vibe coding ships vulnerabilities unreviewed; pitches continuous threat exposure management.

assertions.quote: 46% of AI generated code is reportedly uh contain some form of security weakness

verdicts.note: Veracode 2025 found ~45% of AI-generated samples failed security tests; earlier academic studies of Copilot found similar rates.
AI commits introduce more correctness and security issues than they fix, across all five tools. But about 7.5-14.8% of commits introduce any issue at all, and most issues are smells.

Security risk is the most-cited open challenge (10 of 20 RQ8 sources); peer-reviewed and practitioner sources agree generated code may contain weaknesses when it is not rigorously verified, but no prevalence rate is synthesized.

733 Copilot (and CodeWhisperer, Codeium) snippets found in public GitHub projects: static analysis plus manual filtering flagged CWE weaknesses in 27.3% (about 30% of Python, 25% of JavaScript). Frequent, but these are tool-flagged weaknesses, not confirmed exploits, and there is no human-written baseline.

assertions.quote: Developers admit that they often don't deeply review the AI output

verdicts.note: Surveys (e.g. Sonar 2026) report many developers don't always check AI code before committing, despite saying they distrust it.

The Debt paper says AI-generated code is unlikely to all get thorough review and over-trust raises acceptance. The vibe-coding review also finds code accepted without full understanding. Both are cited, not measured, prevalence.

assertions.quote: over 70% of developers are now using some form of AI coding assistance

verdicts.note: Stack Overflow 2025: ~84% use or plan to use AI tools, about half of professionals daily; JetBrains and DORA report similar figures.

assertions.quote: if you're going to be doing vibe coding in the future, I think CTM is your only option

verdicts.note: Continuous testing helps, but SAST in CI, dependency scanning, code review, secure defaults and threat modeling are also practical; 'only option' is a vendor pitch.

Authors recommend static analysis, security checks and continuous post-merge monitoring because AI-introduced issues persist, but they do not claim or show that continuous automated testing is the only practical approach.

Re-judged: the Debt paper recommends static analysis, tests, security checks and post-merge monitoring together; it does not show that continuous automated security testing is the only way, so it doesn't settle this claim.
